abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Although bulk crystals of lead‐free vacancy‐ordered double perovskites demonstrated a highly efficient emission, their nanocrystals (NCs) counterparts exhibit inferior optical performance. To understand the reasons behind this phenomenon, Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ double perovskite NCs are synthesized, and their optical properties are compared with their bulk powders. Temperature‐dependent spectroscopy revealed that the NCs sustain a thermal sensitization of the intermediate trap state, which is located between the self‐trapped state of the host (Cs2ZrCl6) and the triplet states of the dopant (Te4+). This opens up a pathway for the non‐radiative recombination, and thus decreases the energy transfer efficiency from host to dopant. Importantly, this pathway is suppressed in larger (40 nm) Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs, resulting in their photoluminescence quantum yield of 24%, as compared to 7% for the 22 nm NCs. Furthermore, the emission spectral range of these double perovskite NCs is shown to extended into near‐infrared by incorporating rare‐earth ions as additional dopants. The study has established a crucial relation between the optical properties and the size effect in lead‐free vacancy‐ordered double perovskites and thus lays a foundation for further improvement of their optical performance.

sec.p: Keywords: double perovskites, energy transfer, nanocrystals, optical properties, rare‐earth ion doping

abstract.p: The optical properties of doped‐double perovskites Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+, both the form of nanocrystals (NCs) and bulk powders, are studied and compared. The PLQY of the doped‐NCs decreases with a decrease in size, which contrasts with what is typically observed for semiconductor QDs. Furthermore, the emission spectral range of these double perovskite NCs can be extended into near‐infrared by incorporating rare‐earth ions as additional dopants.

The actual Te/Zr ratios in both bulk samples and NCs are ≈0.1. We note the PL QY is very sensitive to Te doping concentration, and a slight change in doping concentration can significantly affect PL QY.

Temperature‐dependent PL spectra of a) Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs and b) bulk powders excited at 250 nm. c) Temperature‐dependent integrated PL intensity, d) PL peak position, and e) average PL lifetimes of the host (Cs2ZrCl6) and dopant (Te4+) bands for Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs and bulk powders. The blue and red circles correspond to nano and bulk materials, respectively. f) A scheme illustrating possible carrier dynamics in Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs and bulk materials (see text for the related discussion and explanations of acronyms).

sec.p: To prove this hypothesis, we synthesized the Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs with an increased diameter (≈40 vs. ≈22 nm for the samples studied previously). To do so, we first had to identify the surface‐bound ligands limiting the NC growth. The surface chemistry of the initial NC ensemble was studied by means of XPS and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Figure S17a (Supporting Information) demonstrates a series of well‐defined bands at 1460, 1545, and 1710 cm−1 in the FTIR spectra of Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs. The first two bands are attributed to the bending vibration of COO− while the latter belongs to dissociative carbonyl (C = O). This data confirms the presence of OA on the NC surface. Another component of the synthesis that is frequently used as a ligand for lead‐halide perovskites is DDAC. However, the DDAC ligand cannot be identified by any of the conventional infrared spectroscopy methods because of its symmetry. Therefore, high‐resolution XPS has been used with Ar+ sputter etching to remove the surface ligands and reveal the subsurface information for the NCs (Figure S6b and S17b, Supporting Information). Both FTIR and XPS data did now show any detectable amounts of DDAC, indicating that OA is the only ligand capped at the surface of the NCs. The concentration of OA can affect the reaction rate significantly and thus also the size of the particles.

The volume of OA was thus consequently increased from 1 to 4 mL, resulting in an increase of the average size of Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs from 22 to almost 40 nm (Figure
3 ; Figure S18, Supporting Information). While the NC diameter almost doubled, the shape of the NCs evolved from spherical to hexagonal, and further to cubic‐like (Figure 3). Furthermore, the chemical composition slightly shifted toward a more ideal stoichiometric ratio between the elements (Table S3, Supporting Information) due to the lower surface‐to‐volume ratio of the larger NCs. As expected, these changes in the NC sizes did not influence the shape of the absorption and PL spectra, which are mainly defined by the dopant‐related optical transitions (Figure 3e). However, in support of our hypothesis, there is a positive linear dependency between the PL QY at 580 nm and the NC size (Figure 3f). Therefore, the main cause of the decrease of PL with decreasing NC size can be attributed to the energy transfer between the Te4+ and defect state, as elucidated in detail in our previous discussion (and illustrated in Figure 2f).

caption.p: TEM images of Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs produced using different volumes of OA added during standard synthesis: a) 1 mL, b) 2 mL, c) 3 mL, and d) 4 mL. The scale bar is 200 nm for all frames. e) PL (solid lines; excitation is 395 nm), and PLE (dashed lines; emission at 580 nm) spectra of Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs in hexane obtained using different amounts of OA (1–4 mL). f) Close‐to‐linear relationship between the NC size and their PL QY. The blue area represents the width of the NC's size distribution.

PL spectra of a) x%Yb3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs, b) x%Er3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs, and c) x%Nd3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs. PL decay curves of d) x%Yb3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs (1000 nm), e) x%Er3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs (1539 nm), and f) x%Nd3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs (1073 nm) under excitation of 395 nm.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, we have successfully synthesized vacancy‐ordered Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ double perovskite NCs with an average size of 22 nm, and their properties are compared with their bulk counterpart. These NCs exhibit the same crystalline phase and yellow emission as the corresponding bulk powders. The PL of the NCs is more sensitive to thermal quenching than the bulk powders; time‐resolved PL decay measurements demonstrate the appearance of an additional component in the PL dynamics of Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs above 130 K. We conclude that the PL quenching in the case of NCs originates from larger Jahn–Teller distortions and thus the lower surface trap activation in comparison with bulk powders. The hypothesis of the connection between the PL intensity arising from the Te4+ content and the size/stoichiometry of the crystals is supported by the tuning of the size of the Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs from 22 to 40 nm, upon which the PL QY of Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs increased from 7% to 24%. Finally, we also show potential for achieving efficient NIR emission by employing a co‐doping strategy of Cs2ZrCl6:Te4+ NCs with lanthanide ions. Overall, our study addresses the size dependence of the optical properties in vacancy‐ordered perovskites, providing a deeper understanding of fundamental photophysical processes in these materials systems and possible strategies for their broader applications.
